ask.changes_what: Dysuria plus frequency without vaginal symptoms can justify empirical treatment in women; absent or nonspecific symptoms should push toward other causes of fever, AKI or delirium.
ask.do_not_use_when: The LRs apply to non-pregnant women with uncomplicated UTI; do not apply them to men, catheterized patients, or elderly patients with delirium and no new urinary symptoms.
ask.escalation_warning: Urinary symptoms with fever, rigors, flank pain, hypotension or AKI indicate pyelonephritis/urosepsis, which needs cultures, antibiotics and assessment for obstruction.

evidence.citation: Bent S, Nallamothu BK, Simel DL, Fihn SD, Saint S. Does this woman have an acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection? JAMA. 2002;287(20):2701-2710.
evidence.population: Women presenting with one or more symptoms of acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection (9 studies)
evidence.quote: dysuria (summary positive likelihood ratio [LR], 1.5; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.2-2.0)
evidence.reference_standard: Urine culture as defined in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection - finding: dysuria present

evidence.citation: Bent S, Nallamothu BK, Simel DL, Fihn SD, Saint S. Does this woman have an acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection? JAMA. 2002;287(20):2701-2710.
evidence.population: Women presenting with one or more symptoms of acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection (9 studies)
evidence.quote: absence of dysuria (summary negative LR, 0.5; 95% CI, 0.3-0.7)
evidence.reference_standard: Urine culture as defined in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection - finding: dysuria absent

evidence.citation: Bent S, Nallamothu BK, Simel DL, Fihn SD, Saint S. Does this woman have an acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection? JAMA. 2002;287(20):2701-2710.
evidence.population: Women presenting with one or more symptoms of acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection (9 studies)
evidence.reference_standard: Urine culture as defined in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection - finding: frequency present

evidence.citation: Bent S, Nallamothu BK, Simel DL, Fihn SD, Saint S. Does this woman have an acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection? JAMA. 2002;287(20):2701-2710.
evidence.population: Women with UTI symptoms in the single included study that examined symptom combinations
evidence.quote: 24.6 for the combination of dysuria and frequency but no vaginal discharge or irritation
evidence.reference_standard: Urine culture as defined in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection - combination: dysuria and frequency without vaginal discharge or irritation

ask.how: Ask specifically about pain or burning on passing urine, new increase in frequency or urgency, and their onset; then ask about vaginal discharge or irritation, hematuria, flank pain and fever. Establish whether the symptoms are new relative to baseline (important in elderly or catheterized patients).
ask.negative_finding: Absence of dysuria lowers the probability only modestly (LR- 0.5); history alone cannot rule out UTI once one symptom is present.
ask.pitfalls: Vaginitis, urethritis and STIs mimic dysuria (vaginal discharge/irritation LR 0.2-0.3 for UTI). In elderly patients asymptomatic bacteriuria is common, and confusion without new genitourinary symptoms should not be attributed to UTI.
ask.positive_finding: In women, dysuria (LR+ 1.5) or frequency (LR+ 1.8) each raise UTI probability slightly; dysuria and frequency together without vaginal discharge or irritation raise it strongly (LR 24.6, probability above 90%).
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give a reliable history; in delirium, obtain collateral history of new urinary symptoms.
ask.title: Dysuria and urinary frequency/urgency (new)

ask.changes_what: Shaking chills should prompt blood cultures and a search for a bacteremic source (line, biliary, urinary, endovascular); no chills supports withholding cultures when pretest probability is low.
ask.do_not_use_when: The RCE conclusions do not apply to immunocompromised patients or when endocarditis is suspected; in those groups obtain cultures regardless of chills.
ask.escalation_warning: Rigors with hypotension, altered mentation or a central line indicate probable bacteremia/sepsis: cultures, source control and antibiotics within the hour.

evidence.citation: Coburn B, Morris AM, Tomlinson G, Detsky AS. Does this adult patient with suspected bacteremia require blood cultures? JAMA. 2012;308(5):502-511.
evidence.population: Adult immunocompetent patients in whom bacteremia was suspected (35 studies; 4566 bacteremia and 25,946 negative episodes)
evidence.quote: The severity of chills graded on an ordinal scale (shaking chills, LR, 4.7; 95% CI, 3.0-7.2) may be more useful.

evidence.citation: Tokuda Y, Miyasato H, Stein GH, Kishaba T. The degree of chills for risk of bacteremia in acute febrile illness. Am J Med. 2005;118(12):1417.
evidence.population: 526 consecutive adults with acute febrile illness (40, 7.6%, bacteremic)
evidence.quote: Shaking chills showed a specificity of 90.3% (95% CI 89.2-91.5) and positive likelihood ratio of 4.65 (95% CI 2.95-6.86).
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia - finding: shaking chills (whole-body shaking under a thick blanket)

evidence.citation: Tokuda Y, Miyasato H, Stein GH, Kishaba T. The degree of chills for risk of bacteremia in acute febrile illness. Am J Med. 2005;118(12):1417.
evidence.population: 526 consecutive adults with acute febrile illness (40, 7.6%, bacteremic)
evidence.quote: The absence of chills showed a sensitivity of 87.5% (95% CI 74.4-94.5) and negative likelihood ratio of 0.24 (95% CI 0.11-0.51).
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia - finding: any chills (sensitivity and LR- refer to absence of chills)

ask.how: Ask the patient (or witnesses) whether they have had chills and grade the worst episode: mild = feeling cold, needing a jacket; moderate = needing a thick blanket; shaking chills = whole-body shaking even under a thick blanket. Record timing relative to fever and any line, procedure or infusion.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of any chills lowers the probability of bacteremia (LR- 0.24) but does not exclude it, particularly in elderly or immunocompromised patients who may not mount rigors.
ask.pitfalls: Rigors also occur with malaria, transfusion or drug reactions, and after amphotericin or contaminated infusions; the grading relies on patient recall and the RCE data exclude immunocompromised patients and suspected endocarditis.
ask.positive_finding: Shaking (rigor-grade) chills raise the probability of bacteremia about 4.7-fold (LR+ 4.7, 95% CI 3.0-7.2; specificity 0.90) and justify blood cultures before antibiotics.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or witness able to describe the episode; ask before antipyretics blunt recall.
ask.title: Rigors / shaking chills

ask.changes_what: Positive: fingerstick now, treat, and observe for recurrence (sulfonylurea/renal failure -> admit); negative: keep glucose check but move to cardiac/neurologic causes of the spell.
ask.contraindications: None; the history must never delay a point-of-care glucose in any patient with altered mental status, syncope or focal deficit.
ask.do_not_use_when: Never rely on symptom history alone in an obtunded, post-ictal or focally weak patient - measure glucose immediately.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypoglycemia with sulfonylurea, insulin overdose, renal failure or alcohol needs monitored admission and repeated glucose; persistent deficit after glucose correction is a stroke workup.
ask.how: Ask specifically about insulin or sulfonylurea use (drug, dose, timing of last dose), missed or delayed meals, alcohol, recent renal or hepatic decline, and prodromal autonomic symptoms (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger) or neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, drowsiness, difficulty speaking, weakness). Confirm with a fingerstick glucose at the time of symptoms.
ask.negative_finding: No exposure to insulin or secretagogues and no critical illness, cortisol/hormone deficiency or alcohol makes drug-induced hypoglycemia unlikely, but a measured glucose is still required because neuroglycopenia can present without warning symptoms.
ask.pitfalls: Long-standing diabetes and beta-blockers blunt autonomic warning symptoms so neuroglycopenic presentation (confusion, focal deficit) may be the only clue; sulfonylurea hypoglycemia recurs for 24-72 h so a single corrected glucose is not the end of the episode.
ask.positive_finding: Insulin/secretagogue exposure plus a missed meal, alcohol or renal impairment and autonomic or neuroglycopenic prodrome makes hypoglycemia likely; Whipple's triad (symptoms, documented low glucose, resolution with glucose) confirms it.
ask.prerequisites: A collateral history when the patient is confused; the medication list including recently added sulfonylureas, insulin dose changes, or drugs that potentiate them.
ask.title: Hypoglycemia history: insulin/sulfonylurea use, missed meals, adrenergic or neuroglycopenic symptoms

ask.changes_what: Positive: stop or taper the culprit and check sodium; the review is additive to, not a replacement for, the infectious/metabolic delirium workup.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not delay sepsis, hypoglycemia or stroke evaluation while the medication list is being reconciled.
ask.escalation_warning: Abrupt benzodiazepine or opioid withdrawal can itself cause delirium, seizures or severe pain; taper rather than stop in chronic users.
ask.how: Reconcile every current drug (including OTC, PRN and recently stopped) against the admission list and the last 72 h MAR. Flag anticholinergics, benzodiazepines/Z-drugs, opioids, dihydropyridines, antihistamines, steroids, any drug added or dose-changed in the past week, and diuretics/thiazides (sodium).
ask.negative_finding: No culprit drug identified does not exclude delirium or medication effect; look for infection, metabolic and structural causes.
ask.pitfalls: Risk data are relative risks/odds ratios from cohort studies, not diagnostic sensitivity or specificity, so no LR can be assigned. Untreated severe pain also precipitates delirium, so opioids should be tapered rather than abruptly withdrawn.
ask.positive_finding: One or more deliriogenic drugs or a recent addition/dose change temporally preceding the mental-status change. More than three drugs added during admission roughly triples delirium risk in older inpatients.
ask.prerequisites: Reliable medication history from chart, pharmacy record or family; time of each new start or dose change.
ask.title: Deliriogenic medication review: anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids, new/changed drugs, thiazides

examine.changes_what: Positive: label as delirium and work up precipitants; negative: pursue dementia, depression, psychosis or focal neurology but rescreen if course fluctuates.
examine.do_not_use_when: Not a substitute for glucose, vitals, and focal neurological exam in acute mental-status change; use CAM-ICU in ventilated or non-verbal patients.
examine.escalation_warning: A positive CAM with fever, meningism, focal deficit or reduced consciousness needs urgent evaluation for meningitis, stroke or sepsis regardless of screen result.

evidence.citation: Wong CL, Holroyd-Leduc J, Simel DL, Straus SE. Does this patient have delirium?: value of bedside instruments. JAMA 2010;304:779-786.
evidence.population: Hospitalized adults, mostly older medical/surgical inpatients, across 25 prospective studies (N=3027)
evidence.quote: the CAM has the best available supportive data as a bedside delirium instrument (summary-positive LR, 9.6; 95% CI, 5.8-16.0; summary-negative LR, 0.16; 95% CI, 0.09-0.29)
evidence.reference_standard: DSM-based diagnosis by geriatrician, psychiatrist or neurologist

evidence.citation: Shi Q, Warren L, Saposnik G, Macdermid JC. Confusion assessment method: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy. Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat 2013;9:1359-1370.
evidence.location: Abstract, Results; Results text and Figure 2 (bivariate estimate)
evidence.population: Adults in a variety of medical settings; 22 studies of CAM and CAM-ICU (n=2442)
evidence.quote: The pooled sensitivities and specificity for CAM were 82% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 69%-91%) and 99% (95% CI: 87%-100%)

examine.how: After a brief cognitive test (e.g. months backwards, digit span) and interview, score four features: (1) acute onset and fluctuating course from an informant/chart, (2) inattention, (3) disorganized thinking, (4) altered level of consciousness. CAM positive = features 1 AND 2 plus either 3 or 4. Takes about 5 minutes.
examine.negative_finding: Negative CAM lowers the probability substantially (pooled LR- 0.16) but pooled sensitivity is only ~0.82; repeat the screen if fluctuation is suspected.
examine.pitfalls: Accuracy falls with untrained raters and without a formal attention test; dementia, aphasia and hypoactive delirium lower sensitivity. The CAM identifies delirium, not its cause.
examine.positive_finding: Positive CAM makes delirium roughly 10 times more likely (pooled LR+ 9.6) and should trigger a search for the precipitant (infection, drugs, metabolic, withdrawal).
examine.prerequisites: Baseline cognition from a collateral source; trained rater; patient able to respond (use CAM-ICU for intubated/non-verbal patients).
examine.title: Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) delirium screen

examine.changes_what: Miosis + hypoventilation: give naloxone and support ventilation. Eye-movement signs + ataxia/confusion: IV thiamine now, before glucose. Gaze deviation: stroke pathway or EEG.
examine.do_not_use_when: Never withhold thiamine or naloxone because the eye or pupil findings are absent; both treatments are low-risk and the signs are insensitive.
examine.escalation_warning: Hypoventilation with miosis needs airway support and naloxone now; new gaze deviation or ophthalmoplegia with headache or focal deficits needs urgent neuroimaging.

evidence.citation: Harper CG, Giles M, Finlay-Jones R. Clinical signs in the Wernicke-Korsakoff complex: a retrospective analysis of 131 cases diagnosed at necropsy. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry. 1986;49(4):341-345.
evidence.population: 131 cases of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome diagnosed at necropsy, Western Australia, retrospective review of clinical records (80% undiagnosed in life)
evidence.quote: only 16% had the classical clinical triad and 19% had no documented clinical signs
evidence.target_condition: COMPOSITE: classic Wernicke triad (oculomotor abnormality + cerebellar ataxia + altered mental state) all documented antemortem, for necropsy-proven Wernicke-Korsakoff

evidence.citation: Caine D, Halliday GM, Kril JJ, Harper CG. Operational criteria for the classification of chronic alcoholics: identification of Wernicke's encephalopathy. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry. 1997;62(1):51-60.
evidence.population: 106 alcoholics screened from a large necropsy sample; criteria applied retrospectively to patient records by 3 independent raters; subgroup with Wernicke's plus hepatic encephalopathy
evidence.quote: Wernicke's encephalopathy was underrecognized only when occurring with hepatic encephalopathy (50% sensitivity)
evidence.target_condition: COMPOSITE: Caine operational criteria (2 of 4: dietary deficiency, eye signs, cerebellar dysfunction, altered mental state/memory impairment) for neuropathologically confirmed Wernicke's encephalopathy co-occurring with hepatic encephalopathy

examine.how: Measure pupil size and reactivity in dim light, count respiratory rate for a full minute. Test horizontal and vertical pursuit and check for nystagmus, lateral rectus (VI) palsy or conjugate gaze palsy; note any forced gaze deviation at rest. Then test gait or heel-shin for ataxia and screen mental state and short-term recall.
examine.negative_finding: Normal pupils do not exclude opioid effect after mixed ingestions or hypoxia. The full Wernicke triad was documented in only 16% of necropsy-proven cases, so absence of eye signs must not withhold thiamine in at-risk patients.
examine.pitfalls: Miosis also follows pontine stroke, clonidine, organophosphates and cholinergic eye drops; mydriasis after hypoxic arrest can mask opioid miosis. Wernicke's without alcohol (bariatric surgery, hyperemesis, cancer) presents atypically; eye signs are frequently missed on record review.
examine.positive_finding: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory rate <=12 in an unresponsive patient points to opioid toxidrome and justifies naloxone. Nystagmus, VI palsy or gaze palsy plus ataxia or confusion in a malnourished or alcohol-using patient meets Caine criteria for Wernicke's and mandates immediate IV thiamine; forced conjugate gaze deviation suggests stroke or ongoing seizure.
examine.prerequisites: Pen light; ability to open the eyelids; record any recent opioid, sedative or eye-drop exposure and prior ocular surgery.
examine.title: Pupils and eye movements: miosis with hypoventilation (opioid), ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus with ataxia (Wernicke), gaze deviation

examine.changes_what: Fail: proceed to CAM/4AT and search for precipitants (infection, drugs, metabolic). Pass: delirium less likely; if concern persists, repeat later because inattention fluctuates.
examine.contraindications: None; uninterpretable in stupor, aphasia or when the patient cannot communicate.
examine.do_not_use_when: Not interpretable in stupor/coma, aphasia, severe hearing impairment or when the patient cannot communicate; do not label a patient with dementia as delirious on this test alone.
examine.escalation_warning: New inattention with focal signs, fever with neck stiffness, or rapidly declining consciousness needs urgent evaluation for stroke, CNS infection or NCSE rather than a delirium screen alone.

evidence.citation: O'Regan NA, Maughan K, Liddy N et al. Five short screening tests in the detection of prevalent delirium: diagnostic accuracy and performance in different neurocognitive subgroups. International journal of geriatric psychiatry. 2018.
evidence.population: 470 older medical inpatients assessed within 36 h of admission (184 with delirium), Ireland, cross-sectional
evidence.quote: The MOTYB, scored in a binary fashion, also performed well (sensitivity 84.6%, specificity 58.4%, NPV 87.4%, PPV 52.8).
evidence.target_condition: Delirium (Revised Delirium Rating Scale) - months of the year backward scored binary (fail vs pass)

evidence.citation: Marra A, Jackson JC, Ely EW et al. Focusing on Inattention: The Diagnostic Accuracy of Brief Measures of Inattention for Detecting Delirium. Journal of hospital medicine. 2019.
evidence.population: 234 acutely ill ED patients aged >=65 years, academic tertiary ED, USA; inattention tasks administered by a physician
evidence.quote: Making any error on the MOTYB-12 task had a sensitivity of 84.0% (95% CI, 65.4%-93.6%) and specificity of 51.9% (95% CI, 45.2%-58.5%).
evidence.reference_standard: Comprehensive psychiatrist assessment using DSM-IV-TR criteria
evidence.target_condition: Delirium (psychiatrist, DSM-IV-TR) - any error reciting months backward December to January (MOTYB-12)

evidence.citation: Marra A, Jackson JC, Ely EW et al. Focusing on Inattention: The Diagnostic Accuracy of Brief Measures of Inattention for Detecting Delirium. Journal of hospital medicine. 2019.
evidence.population: 234 acutely ill ED patients aged >=65 years, academic tertiary ED, USA
evidence.quote: Making any error on the MOTYB-6 task had a sensitivity of 80.0% (95% confidence interval [CI], 60.9%-91.1%) and specificity of 57.1% (95% CI, 50.4%- 63.7%).
evidence.reference_standard: Comprehensive psychiatrist assessment using DSM-IV-TR criteria
evidence.target_condition: Delirium (psychiatrist, DSM-IV-TR) - any error reciting months backward December to July (MOTYB-6)

evidence.citation: Hasemann W, Grossmann FF, Bingisser R et al. Optimizing the month of the year backwards test for delirium screening of older patients in the emergency department. The American journal of emergency medicine. 2020.
evidence.population: ED patients aged >=65 years, single-centre prospective mCAM-ED validation cohort, Switzerland; test administered by trained nurse research assistants
evidence.quote: achieved with the month of September resulting in an overall sensitivity of 0.90 and an overall specificity of 0.89
evidence.reference_standard: Geriatrician delirium assessment within 1 h of the index test
evidence.target_condition: Delirium (geriatrician reference assessment) - months backward scored as 'last month in correct order', fail = not reaching September

evidence.citation: Hasemann W, Grossmann FF, Bingisser R et al. Optimizing the month of the year backwards test for delirium screening of older patients in the emergency department. The American journal of emergency medicine. 2020.
evidence.population: ED patients aged >=65 years, single-centre prospective mCAM-ED validation cohort, Switzerland
evidence.quote: achieved when 8 or more errors were reached resulting in an overall sensitivity of 0.95 and overall specificity of 0.94
evidence.reference_standard: Geriatrician delirium assessment within 1 h of the index test
evidence.target_condition: Delirium (geriatrician reference assessment) - months backward scored by number of errors, fail = 8 or more errors

evidence.citation: Voyer P, Champoux N, Desrosiers J et al. Assessment of inattention in the context of delirium screening: one size does not fit all! International psychogeriatrics. 2017.
evidence.population: 191 older adults with or without cognitive impairment in one acute care hospital and one long-term care facility, Canada (secondary analysis)
evidence.quote: showed the best balance between sensitivity and specificity (82.6%; 95% CI [61.2-95.0], and 62.5%; 95% CI [54.7-69.8] respectively) for the entire group
evidence.reference_standard: DSM-5 delirium criteria (CAM used to elicit symptoms)
evidence.target_condition: Delirium (DSM-5) - months of the year backward, fail = not completed successfully

evidence.citation: Tieges Z, Maclullich AMJ, Anand A et al. Diagnostic accuracy of the 4AT for delirium detection in older adults: systematic review and meta-analysis. Age and ageing. 2021.
evidence.population: Pooled 17 diagnostic accuracy studies, 3,702 observations, older adults >=65 in acute medicine, surgery, ED and care home
evidence.quote: The pooled sensitivity was 0.88 (95% CI 0.80-0.93) and the pooled specificity was 0.88 (95% CI 0.82-0.92).
evidence.reference_standard: Standard diagnostic criteria (DSM/ICD) or validated delirium tool
evidence.target_condition: COMPOSITE: 4AT score >=4 (alertness, AMT4, months backward attention item, acute change/fluctuation) for delirium

examine.how: Ask the patient to recite the months of the year backward starting from December. Common scorings: any error or failure to complete (binary); number of errors; or the last month reached in correct order (reaching September or beyond = pass). Digit span (forward/backward) is an alternative but performs less well in isolation.
examine.negative_finding: Correct completion lowers the probability of delirium (LR- roughly 0.1-0.3 across studies) but does not exclude hypoactive delirium; specificity is modest (0.5-0.6 with any-error scoring in mixed inpatients) because dementia, low education and drowsiness also cause failure.
examine.pitfalls: Patients with dementia fail without delirium; specificity is poor in cognitively impaired populations. Scoring method changes performance markedly (any error vs >=8 errors vs September cut-off), so record which rule you used.
examine.positive_finding: Failure (any error or not reaching September) indicates inattention, the core feature of delirium; sensitivity for delirium is about 0.80-0.95 depending on setting and scoring, so it is a useful first-stage screen that should be followed by a full assessment (CAM/4AT, DSM criteria).
examine.prerequisites: Patient awake enough to engage, able to hear and speak (or write); language and education considered.
examine.title: Attention test: months of the year backward / digit span

examine.changes_what: Present: escalate now (continuous monitoring, blood gas, bronchodilator/NIV or airway plan). Absent: do not use to downgrade severity; rely on oximetry, gas and peak flow.
examine.contraindications: None; it is observation only. Do not delay oxygen, bronchodilator or airway management to complete the assessment.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of the sign to withhold escalation in a drowsy, exhausted or silent-chest patient.
examine.escalation_warning: Accessory muscle use plus inability to speak, drowsiness, silent chest, bradycardia or SpO2 <90% = life-threatening exacerbation: immediate senior/ICU involvement.
examine.how: Observe from the doorway before touching the patient: sternocleidomastoid/scalene contraction on inspiration, suprasternal or intercostal retraction, tripod posture, pursed-lip exhalation, and diaphoresis. Ask an open question and note whether the patient can finish a sentence in one breath (sentences vs phrases vs single words).
examine.negative_finding: Absence of accessory muscle use does not exclude significant airflow limitation or hypercapnia; a tiring or obtunded patient may lose the sign as ventilatory failure develops.
examine.pitfalls: Loss of accessory muscle use with rising drowsiness signals fatigue, not improvement. Obesity, a thick neck and supine positioning hide sternocleidomastoid contraction.
examine.positive_finding: Visible accessory muscle use, tripoding or speech limited to words/phrases marks a severe exacerbation of airflow obstruction (asthma/COPD) or another cause of high work of breathing, and in admitted asthmatics is associated with a markedly lower %FEV1. Treat it as a severity marker, not as a discriminator between causes.
examine.prerequisites: Patient undressed enough to see the neck and chest wall; observe at rest before any intervention if safe to do so.
examine.title: Work of breathing: accessory muscle use, tripoding, pursed-lip breathing, inability to speak full sentences

modifiers: admitted this afternoon for COPD exacerbation
